title: Cat-hole latrine: where to dig it and how to use it
asks: how to dig a cat hole
how deep should a cat hole be
where do i poop in the woods
how far from water should i go to the bathroom
no toilet what do we do with human waste
how far should the latrine be from camp and water
how to bury poop when camping
no latrine at this site, how do we handle human waste, over
answer: Do not soil the ground in the camp area with urine or feces. When no latrine is available, dig a cat hole and cover your waste. The Army uses the cat-hole latrine when a unit is on the move.

Pick the spot away from water. The Army survival manual says to locate latrines 200 feet from water and away from shelter. The Army field sanitation manual says at least 100 feet from any ground water source, and downslope from wells, springs, streams and other water sources (30 meters or more).

Keep it away from food: at least 300 feet downwind and downhill from where food is prepared and served. Another passage of the same manual says as far from food operations as possible (100 meters or more).
Do not dig down to the ground water level, or in a place where the contents may drain into a water source.
Dig a hole about one foot deep and one foot in diameter.
After using the cat hole, fill it in completely and pack the dirt down.
Wash or sanitize your hands after using the latrine.
warnings: The Army manuals say the use of improvised latrines such as cat holes is generally prohibited in the United States, and that it has become less common due to ecological and statutory restrictions.

quotes.text: Do not soil the ground in the camp area with urine or feces; use latrines. When no latrines are available, isolated persons should dig "cat holes" and cover their waste.
Locate latrines 200 feet from water and away from shelter.
Considerations for the placement of latrines. Latrines must be
Located at least 300 feet downwind and downhill from unit food service facilities and at least 100 feet from any unit ground water source.
Latrines are not dug to the ground water level or in places where pit contents may drain into the water source.

Select location for field latrines as follows: As far from food operations as possible (100 meters or more). Downwind and downslope, if possible. Downslope from wells, springs, streams, and other water sources (30 meters or more).
The cat-hole latrine is used when the unit is on the move
The cat-hole latrine is simply a hole approximately one foot deep and one foot in diameter. After using a cat hole it must be completely filled in and the dirt packed down.
When to wash and or sanitize the hands (at a minimum)— Before eating or snacking. After eating or snacking. Before handling and or preparing food. After using the latrine.

Generally, the use of improvised latrines in the U.S. is prohibited. The use of improvised latrines such as cat holes and slit trenches has become less common due to ecological and statutory restrictions.
The types of improvised latrines listed below can be used for field use. Generally, the use of improvised latrines in the United States is prohibited.

conflict: Distance from water differs between Army manuals: ATP 3-50.21 (2018) 'Locate latrines 200 feet from water'; ATP 4-25.12 (2014, change 2 2025) and TB MED 593 (2006) 'at least 100 feet from any unit ground water source'; ATP 4-25.12 also says 'Downslope from wells, springs, streams, and other water sources (30 meters or more)' and 'at least 30 meters down gradient from any ground water source'; TB MED 577 (2010) says 'at least 30 yards (yd) downgradient'. Distance from food: ATP 4-25.12 gives both 'at least 300 feet' and '100 meters or more'. The card shows the figures side by side; the owner must choose.

review.notes: Fail. Drafter flag verdicts: (a) Distance conflict - correctly shown attributed (ATP 3-50.21 200 ft; ATP 4-25.12 and TB MED 593 at least 100 ft and 30 m down-gradient; TB MED 577 30 yd recorded in conflict); keep side by side. Line 3's first sentence should also name its manual ('The Army field sanitation manual says at least 300 feet downwind and downhill from food; another passage of it says 100 meters or more'). (b) 'Generally prohibited in the U.S.' - military context misapplied to a civilian. TC 4-02.3 2-27 and TB MED 593 6-2 speak about Army units on field training exercises (same sections: DOD environmental compliance, chemical latrines 'preferred... during field training exercises', 'Commanders should consult with... garrison environmental authorities'). As written, the warning tells a civilian that digging a cat hole is generally illegal in the U.S., which the sources do not say, and it would discourage safe waste disposal in an emergency. Fix: remove it, or keep its context: 'For Army units training in the U.S., improvised latrines such as cat holes are generally not allowed because of ecological and statutory restrictions.' (TB MED 593 6-1 adds that disposal must follow 'local, state, Federal, and host nation regulatory requirements'.) Other lines verified: do not soil the camp area, cat hole when on the move, not to ground-water level or where it drains to water, 1 ft deep by 1 ft across, fill and pack, wash hands after. Optional: TB MED 593 'at least 100 feet from billeting' supports 'away from shelter'.
